howItWorks.intro: This calculator applies three distinct calculations to your inputs: it isolates the dollar amount actually exposed to the decline (balance × stock allocation), estimates how long a loss of that size has historically taken markets to recover based on the depth of past drawdowns, and separately shows what the same dollar loss would compound to by your target retirement date if it were never recovered at all. Comparing the "permanent loss" figure against the "with recovery" figure is usually the most telling part of the output, because it puts a dollar amount on the cost of panic-selling rather than leaving it as a vague warning.
rules: Today's Loss = 401k Balance x Stock Allocation % x Market Drop %
Future Impact = Lost Amount x (1 + Avg Return)^Years (compounding the loss forward)
Recovery times based on historical S&P 500 drawdown analysis
Days of Contributions = Today's Loss / (Monthly Contribution / 22 workdays)
howItWorks.outro: Treat every figure here as an illustration of how volatility and compounding interact, not as a forecast of your account's actual future value — real markets don't move in straight lines, and a flat average-return assumption smooths over the exact kind of sequence-of-returns risk this tool is meant to surface. None of this is personalized financial advice; decisions about withdrawals, rebalancing, or allocation changes deserve a look at your full financial picture, timeline, and risk tolerance, including a licensed advisor if the dollar amounts involved matter enough to you.

faq.question: Should I sell my 401(k) holdings when the market drops?
faq.answer: Selling converts a paper loss into a permanent one and removes you from the eventual rebound, which is the part of the cycle that does most of the long-term rebuilding. Historically, a large share of a decade's total market gains has arrived in a small handful of trading sessions, often clustered right after the sharpest declines — an investor who moves to cash during a downturn and waits for things to feel safe again routinely misses several of those sessions. None of this makes a drop pleasant to watch; it just means the account impact of selling is usually larger than the impact of the drop itself.

faq.question: How long does it typically take the market to recover from a drop?
faq.answer: Depth matters more than the headline percentage suggests. Shallow pullbacks around 5% have historically resolved within weeks; 10% corrections have typically worked themselves out within a few months; 20% bear markets have more often taken over a year; declines beyond 30%, like 2008 or early 2020, have taken anywhere from under a year to several years depending on the cause. Every major U.S. market decline on record has eventually been followed by new highs, though "eventually" is doing real work in that sentence and is not a guarantee for any specific future event.

faq.question: Does it make sense to keep contributing during a downturn?
faq.answer: For money with a long time horizon, continuing regular contributions through a decline means each paycheck buys more shares at a lower price — the mechanical upside of dollar-cost averaging. This logic only applies to money you won't need for years; funds earmarked for near-term expenses shouldn't be exposed to stock market swings in the first place, regardless of where prices currently sit.

faq.question: How much could a crash actually cost a 401(k) balance?
faq.answer: It scales directly with how much of the account sits in stocks. A portfolio that's effectively 100% equities could see a 30–50% decline in a severe, multi-year bear market, while a 60/40 stock-bond mix has historically held losses closer to 15–25% in the same environment because the bond portion cushions the blow. On a $250,000 balance, that's the difference between an all-stock account falling toward $125,000–$175,000 versus a balanced account landing nearer $187,500–$212,500 — allocation matters as much as the severity of the crash itself.

faq.question: What is sequence-of-returns risk, and why does it come up with retirement accounts specifically?
faq.answer: It refers to the fact that identical average returns can produce very different ending balances depending on the order those returns arrive in, once withdrawals enter the picture. A retiree pulling a fixed dollar amount out of a shrinking account during a downturn sells more shares per dollar withdrawn than they would at higher prices, permanently reducing the shares left to participate in the eventual recovery. Someone still contributing benefits from the same drop instead, because they're adding shares at the discount rather than removing them. It's the main reason that advice reasonable for a 30-year-old can be exactly backwards for someone five years from drawing on the account.

faq.question: What does a 20% market drop actually look like in dollars on a typical account?
faq.answer: Take a $250,000 balance with a common 80/20 stock-to-bond split. A 20% equity decline applies only to the stock portion, so the loss works out to roughly $250,000 × 0.80 × 0.20 = $40,000, leaving a balance near $210,000 — not the $50,000 a quick guess based on the headline percentage might suggest. Left invested rather than sold, that $210,000 needs about a 19% gain to get back to even; at a 7% average annual return, that's on the order of two and a half years of growth, faster still if contributions continue along the way. This is an illustration of the mechanics, not a prediction for any individual account, and shouldn't be read as a recommendation about what to do with your own money. The number worth sitting with isn't the headline drop — it's the gap between the paper loss and what selling would make permanent.

sections.title: What a Market Drop Actually Does to Your 401(k)
sections.body: A headline saying the S&P 500 fell 20% does not mean your retirement account fell by the same amount. Your actual dollar loss depends on how much of your balance sits in stocks versus bonds, cash, or stable-value funds. Hold $250,000 in a 401(k) with 80% in equities, and a 20% market decline translates to roughly $250,000 × 0.80 × 0.20 = $40,000 in paper losses — not $50,000. The remaining 20% of the portfolio, assuming it's parked in bonds or cash, is largely untouched by the equity sell-off, which is one reason a diversified allocation matters even for savers decades from retirement. That $40,000 is a paper loss, not a realized one; it only becomes permanent if those shares are sold near the bottom. Left invested, a balance that drops from $250,000 to $210,000 needs to grow back by about 19% to return to its starting point. At a 7% average annual return — a reasonable long-run assumption for a diversified, stock-heavy portfolio — that recovery takes roughly two and a half years of growth alone, and considerably less time if payroll contributions keep buying shares along the way.

sections.title: Sequence-of-Returns Risk: Why Timing a Drop Matters as Much as Its Size
sections.body: The order in which gains and losses arrive matters nearly as much as their average, a dynamic known as sequence-of-returns risk, and it cuts in opposite directions depending on which side of retirement you're on. During the accumulation years, a steep drop early on is arguably a gift: every paycheck buys shares at depressed prices, and decades of compounding have time to work in your favor before you need the money. During the withdrawal years, the same drop is far more dangerous — selling shares to fund living expenses while prices are down locks in losses permanently and shrinks the base left to participate in the recovery, a pattern that has derailed retirement plans that looked perfectly fine on paper using only average-return assumptions. This calculator separates today's paper loss from the longer-run trajectory so both effects are visible side by side. It's meant as an illustration of how volatility and compounding interact, not as a prediction of what any specific account will do or as a recommendation about what you should do with your own money — for decisions with real stakes, that's worth working through with a fuller picture of your finances and, where the amounts are meaningful, with a licensed professional.
